steps: Press your thumbs together with the other fingers tucked into loose fists.
Hold the joined hands a few inches in front of your chest or upper belly.
Push both hands smoothly forward about six inches, away from your body.
Keep both palms angled downward for the whole forward glide.
Hold a steady, determined face — the motion says the action keeps going.
tip: Past form of “Continue” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Point your non-dominant index finger straight up in front of your chest, like a small post.
Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended and spread.
Bring the V hand down over the upright finger so the finger rests between the two prongs.
Aim the V fingertips downward as the hand settles onto the finger.
Keep a businesslike, neutral expression — this is the paperwork version of apply.
tip: “Applies” is signed with the base APPLY sign.

steps: Point your non-dominant index finger straight up in front of your chest, like a small post.
Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended and spread.
Bring the V hand down over the upright finger so the finger rests between the two prongs.
Aim the V fingertips downward as the hand settles onto the finger.
Keep a businesslike, neutral expression — this is the paperwork version of apply.
tip: “Applying” is signed with the base APPLY sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger together into a small pincer, like holding a stamp.
Raise your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest, palm angled sideways.
Tap the pinching hand once against the side of the upright finger.
Angle the pinching hand's palm toward the finger as it taps.
Keep your face neutral — one tap names the machine that prints.
tip: Plural of “Printer” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you, flat and open with the palm facing down.
Rest the fingertips of your dominant hand on the back of that hand, starting in a flat O handshape.
Slide the dominant hand outward across the back of the base hand while opening it into a spread five handshape.
Repeat the short outward slide a second time — the noun form uses two quick movements.
Keep both palms facing down the whole time, as if laying opinions out on a table for someone.
tip: Plural of “Advice” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both hands into tight A fists, pressing each thumb firmly against the folded index finger.
Raise your right A fist to your chest and your left A fist to the left side of your abdomen.
Start with both fists hovering about two inches out from your body.
Thump both fists inward against your body twice in a quick in-out-in double motion.
Keep both palms facing toward your body for the entire movement, like gripping a rifle.
Hold a straight, upright posture with a serious, matter-of-fact expression.
tip: Plural of “Military” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, spreading your fingers wide apart.
Hold both hands about an inch in front of your upper chest, thumbs closest to your body.
Brush both hands straight down your chest as if smoothing a shirt, letting the thumbs drag lightly.
Repeat the downward brush a second time in a quick double movement.
Angle your palms slightly toward yourself so the thumbs stay near your chest as they slide.
Keep a neutral expression — actual chest contact is optional; the double brush is what counts.
tip: Plural of “Clothing” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch the tip of your dominant index finger to your right temple to begin.
Slide your dominant hand downward while changing the index finger into an "F" handshape.
Raise your non-dominant hand into a matching "F" handshape beside the moving hand.
When both hands reach lower-chest level, drop them sharply downward a few inches and stop dead.
tip: Plural of “Decision” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand at the large knuckle so its tip points downward.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing up.
Circle the bent middle-finger tip above the upturned palm, then plant the fingertip into its center.
Hold the planted fingertip still for a moment to mark the exact middle point.
tip: Plural of “Middle” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point both index fingers forward so the two fingertips aim toward each other.
Rotate the two index fingers around one another in a small circular motion.
Draw both hands toward your body in one smooth arcing movement.
Keep your palms angled inward toward yourself as the hands arrive near your chest.
tip: “Comings” is signed with the base COMING sign.

steps: Form an "L" handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb and index finger.
Place the "L" handshape against your chin with the index finger touching the chin.
Bounce the hand gently on your chin two times while keeping the "L" handshape firm.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your face throughout the two bounces.
tip: Plural of “Lesbian” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them in front of your chest.
Angle the fists toward each other so the knuckles face inward like meshing gears.
Interlock the fingers loosely, then move the hands back and forth in small alternating twists.
Keep the movement compact and rhythmic, as if you are turning a set of gears.
tip: Plural of “Machine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both hands into loose fists with each thumb sticking straight up, like signing the number ten.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of your chest, thumb up, as the person being followed.
Set your dominant fist a few inches directly behind the non-dominant one, also thumb up.
Move both fists forward together a short distance, keeping the dominant hand trailing behind the other.
Keep both palms facing sideways and your thumbs upright for the whole forward motion.
Look steadily forward as the hands move, as if watching the person ahead of you.
tip: “Follows” is signed with the base FOLLOW sign.

steps: Raise your non-dominant forearm upright in front of your chest, elbow low, like a tree trunk.
Curve your dominant hand into a C, with the thumb and fingers forming a firm half circle.
Rest the wrist of the C hand on top of the upright forearm.
Rock the C hand left and right twice from the wrist, with the same sway as the sign for TREE.
Keep the trunk arm perfectly still so that only the C hand does the moving.
tip: Plural of “Christmas” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Press your dominant thumb against your index fingertip to form a small pinching shape.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest, facing an imaginary row of options.
Close the fingers onto one option and lift the hand upward and toward your chest.
Angle your palm downward while you draw the selected option inward.
Finish with a small decisive nod of the head, since choosing is an intentional and confident act.
tip: Plural of “Choice” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Cross the middle finger of your dominant hand over its index finger to form an R.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing upward like a paper form.
Lay the R hand down across the fingers of the open palm.
Lift the R, shift it a couple of inches toward the wrist, and set it down again.
Make the double stamp motion with a matter-of-fact expression, as if handling paperwork.
tip: Plural of “Registration” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an 'I love you' handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb, index finger, and pinkie.
Hold the hand in the space in front of your shoulder at about chest height.
Glide the hand forward twice in short, even movements, as if a plane were cruising onward.
Keep your palm facing the floor through the entire movement.
Look in the direction your hand travels with a relaxed, neutral expression.
tip: Plural of “Airport” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, as your canvas.
Make an 'I' handshape with your dominant hand, extending only your pinkie finger.
Touch the pad of your pinkie to the flat palm and draw a few short strokes, as if sketching with a pencil.
Then add the person marker: hold both flat hands out at your sides with fingers pointing outward.
Sweep both flat hands straight down along your torso, keeping the palms facing each other.
Finish the movement with a slight nod, as if presenting the finished artist.
tip: Plural of “Artist” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other three fingers.
Hold the hand out at chest height with the palm facing forward.
Wave the hand from side to side a couple of times using small, tight movements.
Keep the path strictly side to side and never let the hand circle.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression while signing.
tip: Plural of “Furniture” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other fingers.
Touch the 'F' hand against your chest or torso where a shirt button would sit.
Arc the hand downward a few inches along your torso.
Touch your torso again to mark the position of a second button.
Repeat once more to show a third button if you want to show several.
Keep a neutral expression and let the taps mark each button's place.
tip: Plural of “Button” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands flat and open, with the fingers extended and together.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, near your ears or temples.
Move both hands forward together in one short, even motion.
Keep the palms facing each other as the hands travel forward.
Direct your eyes and attention forward, showing concentration on the task.
tip: “Focuses” is signed with the base FOCUS sign.

steps: Form a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers pressed together and the thumb resting along the side.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near your cheek or temple.
Rest the side of your head against the hand, tilting slightly as if settling onto a pillow.
Keep the palm facing toward your face with the fingers pointing toward your ear.
Hold the position briefly with a relaxed face, as if you are ready to fall asleep.
tip: Plural of “Bed” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend the middle finger of your dominant hand while the other fingers stay loosely curled.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward like a tray.
Press the middle fingertip into the center of the palm and rock the hand side to side twice.
Keep your dominant palm angled downward as the middle finger pivots in place.
Use a small, relaxed rocking motion — a stiff, wide sweep reads as a different sign.
tip: Plural of “Medicine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a Y, extending the thumb and pinky while tucking the middle fingers.
Hold the Y handshape beside your head, with the thumb near your ear and the pinky toward your mouth.
Rock the hand with a small double movement, tilting it slightly forward and back twice.
Keep the thumb and pinky extended throughout — folding them in changes the sign entirely.
Keep your face neutral and conversational; TELEPHONE is a plain noun sign.
tip: Plural of “Telephone” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into an E handshape, fingers bent with the thumb tucked beneath them.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing upward like a tray.
Tap the dominant E hand down onto the non-dominant palm two times, with a short bounce between taps.
Keep the dominant palm facing upward as it lands, so the curled fingers do the tapping.
Hold an assertive, serious expression — this sign presents something as a proven fact.
tip: Plural of “Evidence” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Spread your dominant hand into an open 5-handshape with all fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal at chest height, palm turned toward your torso.
Draw the dominant hand downward across the flat hand while wiggling all four fingers like falling drops.
Face both palms toward your own torso as the dominant hand slides down.
Do the downward wiggle once or twice depending on the sentence — twice suggests a continuing flow.
tip: Plural of “Blood” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands as flat open hands, fingers together with thumbs alongside.
Hold both hands up in the neutral signing space in front of your shoulders.
Move both hands forward together in one smooth, straight motion.
Keep both palms facing each other, like the two walls of a corridor.
Use one firm forward push and keep your expression neutral throughout.
tip: Plural of “Hall” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a counter.
Bring your dominant flat hand down to land on it, palm facing down.
Flip the dominant hand over so its back lands on the same palm again.
Make both landings firm and quick using a small wrist flip.
Keep your body relaxed; no extra ROOM sign is needed after this sign.
tip: Plural of “Kitchen” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a hooked two, with the index and middle fingers bent like claws.
Start the hand off to one side of your body at about chest height.
Swing the hand across to the other side in a smooth downward arc.
Keep the palm angled down toward the floor through the whole arc.
Finish with one confident sweep; a single trip from side to side.
tip: “Transfers” is signed with the base TRANSFER sign.

steps: Raise your dominant hand beside your head, forming a loose open hand with the fingers slightly curved.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near the top where the hair sits.
Brush the hand downward along the side of your head, as if smoothing a lock of hair.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your head through the whole downward stroke.
Keep your expression neutral, and let the motion stay close to the head instead of floating out wide.
tip: Plural of “Hair” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers together and pointing straight up.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the upright fingertips nearly touching at the center.
Move the two hands outward to opposite sides, opening a wide flat span like a wall rising.
Keep the palms facing forward, away from your body, for the whole outward movement.
Hold a neutral expression and keep the hands at chest height; the sign simply depicts the flat surface.
tip: Plural of “Wall” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point both index fingers upward with your other fingers curled into loose fists.
Hold both hands in front of your torso at about chest height.
Twist your wrists as you trace two small upward arcs through the air.
Let each fingertip draw a loose cursive W shape, moving upward and outward.
Keep both palms angled toward each other with the fingers leading the motion.
Pair the sign with a bright, satisfied expression to show a good outcome.
tip: Plural of “Success” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Start with your dominant hand a few inches in front of your chest.
Shape the hand like a loose grip, as if about to unscrew a light bulb.
Move the hand inward until the thumb side approaches your chest.
Close the fingers into a flattened O as the hand reaches your body.
End with the flat of your thumbnail touching your chest, fingertips meeting.
Keep a matter-of-fact expression; this sign claims possession of something.
tip: Plural of “Owner” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a loose four hand with your dominant hand, fingers together and thumb tucked.
Hold the hand beside your lower cheek, near the chin, palm facing sideways.
Shake the hand downward twice in two small, quick strokes.
Keep the strokes short — about an inch — right against the cheek.
Use a neutral expression; context separates this from the color brown.
Some signers circle a W handshape at the cheek instead — know both, use the common one.
tip: Plural of “Wine” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into loose 5 handshapes with the fingers spread and slightly bent.
Hold both hands up at chest height in front of your body, palms facing each other.
Point the fingertips of each hand toward the fingertips of the other hand, picturing lanes of cars.
Move the hands back and forth past each other in small alternating motions, like vehicles streaming in opposite lanes.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole alternating movement.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — the sign simply names the condition of traffic.
tip: Plural of “Traffic” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in flat B handshapes with your thumbs resting alongside your fingers, not forming P shapes.
Raise both hands to the neutral signing space in front of your chest with your palms facing each other.
Move both hands straight downward a few inches together in one smooth, level motion.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other and both hands moving evenly as they drop.
Keep your expression neutral and avoid any initialized P handshape when you use this sign alone.
tip: Plural of “Agent” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into flattened-O handshapes, with fingertips and thumbs rounded together.
Hold both hands up near your head, starting at about forehead height in front of you.
Push both hands forward away from your head, pull them slightly back, then push forward again in a double movement.
Keep your palms turned slightly inward toward each other as your hands travel outward.
Use the double movement only for the ongoing process of teaching; one quick movement means the verb teach.
tip: Plural of “Teaching” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat in a B handshape and keep your non-dominant hand flat and still beside it.
Raise your dominant hand to chest height in front of you, starting with the palm facing forward.
Swing your dominant hand outward as if opening a door, then swing it back inward to close it, using two movements.
Keep your palm facing forward the whole time and let your pinkie-side edge act as the door's hinge.
Keep your face neutral; depending on context this same sign can also mean closet, cupboard, or cabinet.
tip: Plural of “Door” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you with your index fingers extended straight and pointing upward.
Curl both index fingers into X handshapes as you begin moving both hands downward together.
Draw the path of a question mark in the air with your moving hands, then open both into palm-down 5 hands to dot it.
Keep your palms facing downward as the 5 handshapes finish the sign in the neutral signing space.
Maintain a thoughtful, inquisitive expression while the hands trace the question-mark shape.
tip: Plural of “Testing” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hook your dominant index finger over your thumb to form an X handshape, folding the remaining fingers down.
Place the hooked X hand just under your chin, close to the front of your throat.
Flick the X hand forward about three inches with a quick wrist motion, then repeat the flick once more.
Angle your palm slightly downward so the hooked X points forward as it slides away from your throat.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply names the material.
tip: Plural of “Metal” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Spread the fingers of both hands wide into open five handshapes.
Raise both hands to chest height in front of you, with all the fingers pointing upward.
Push the hands together so the fingertips interlock, like two opposing scrimmage lines clashing at the snap.
Ram the hands together twice in a quick double movement, keeping the fingers meshed.
Keep the palms facing each other through both rams of the sign.
Hold a neutral, game-ready expression — the double clash is part of the sign.
tip: Plural of “Football” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve the fingers of both hands into loose bent handshapes, with the fingertips pointing downward.
Raise both bent hands to the tops of your shoulders, close to your neck.
Touch the fingertips down onto your shoulders, then lift and touch again with a firm double tap.
Keep the palms angled inward toward your chest through both contacts.
Hold a steady, earnest expression — the repeated tap marks this as a duty.
tip: Plural of “Responsibility” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: “Trusting” is signed with the base TRUST sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: Past form of “Trust” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of your torso with all fingers and thumbs spread loosely apart.
Bring the hands toward each other at chest height until the fingertips of both hands meet in the middle.
Tap the fingertips of both hands together once, as if many people are gathering into one group.
Angle the palms toward each other and slightly downward as the fingertips touch.
Keep a neutral, informative expression instead of the raised-eyebrow look of a question.
tip: Plural of “Session” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Relax both hands into open 5 handshapes, fingers together and slightly loose, with the thumbs ready.
Hold both hands at chest height with the thumbs aimed at your upper chest.
Poke your upper chest twice with both thumb tips, moving the hands forward and back with each poke.
Angle both palms inward toward your body so the thumbs can reach the chest squarely.
Keep your face relaxed and easy, matching the carefree time-off feeling.
tip: Plural of “Vacation” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved open.
Hold the C in front of your body at chest height, slightly to your dominant side.
Trace a quick small circle with the C hand, moving clockwise from your own point of view.
Keep the hand upright with the opening of the C facing outward toward your audience as you circle.
Mouth the word 'century' while signing, since viewers usually need the sentence context to catch it.
tip: Plural of “Century” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a loose A fist, keeping the thumb sticking up and slightly out.
Rest that fist on the open palm of your flat non-dominant hand, held at about waist height.
Lift both hands upward together a few inches, as if boosting the fist from below.
Keep the non-dominant palm facing up so it visibly supports the raised fist.
Aim the sign toward the person you mean: start near yourself for 'I help you', near them for 'you help me'.
tip: Plural of “Assistance” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Flatten both hands with fingers together and thumbs tucked, palms facing the ground.
Raise the flat hands to about waist height, keeping them low in front of your body.
Touch the fingertips of the two hands together in the center to form one level plane.
Sweep both hands smoothly outward to the sides, spreading them wide like laying a surface.
Follow the sweep with your eyes and keep a neutral face, letting the wide flat motion carry the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Floor” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an F, thumb and index touching as if pinching a tiny ring.
Hold your non-dominant hand up with the fingers extended so the ring finger is easy to see.
Slide the F handshape down along the non-dominant ring finger, setting the imaginary band onto it.
Pause briefly with the F handshape resting at the base of the finger to show the ring in place.
Keep the non-dominant hand still and your face neutral, letting the F handshape tell the jewelry story.
tip: Plural of “Ring” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open at chest height, fingers together and pointing forward.
Form an X handshape with your dominant hand by hooking the index finger over the thumb.
Move the dominant X hand firmly toward the open base palm until it makes contact.
Draw the X hand back toward your body slightly right after contact to complete the demand.
Keep your expression serious throughout; a firm face matches the weight of an obligation.
tip: “Requires” is signed with the base REQUIRE sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open at chest height, fingers together and pointing forward.
Form an X handshape with your dominant hand by hooking the index finger over the thumb.
Move the dominant X hand firmly toward the open base palm until it makes contact.
Draw the X hand back toward your body slightly right after contact to complete the demand.
Keep your expression serious throughout; a firm face matches the weight of an obligation.
tip: “Requiring” is signed with the base REQUIRE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open at chest height, fingers together and pointing forward.
Form an X handshape with your dominant hand by hooking the index finger over the thumb.
Move the dominant X hand firmly toward the open base palm until it makes contact.
Draw the X hand back toward your body slightly right after contact to complete the demand.
Keep your expression serious throughout; a firm face matches the weight of an obligation.
tip: Past form of “Require” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold your dominant hand in a loose open shape with the fingers relaxed and slightly spread.
Start the hand near your chest at mid-torso height, as if you are just inside a building.
Sweep the hand upward and outward in a rising arc toward the open space ahead of you.
Repeat the up-and-out sweep a second time with a quick beat to name the noun outdoors.
Aim your gaze toward the open space as you sign, since the eyes help mark the outside area.
tip: Plural of “Outdoor” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form a P handshape with your dominant hand, tucking the thumb between the middle and index fingers with the palm facing down.
Hold the P hand out in neutral space in front of your chest, keeping it steady at chest height.
Move the hand in a small smooth circle, repeating the circling motion twice for emphasis.
Keep the palm facing downward throughout the entire circling movement.
Hold a neutral expression, since the initialized handshape and the circling motion carry the whole meaning.
tip: Plural of “Protein” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, keeping the fingers loosely spread and natural.
Lift both arms and cross them over your chest, the right hand coming to rest near the left shoulder.
Land both open hands gently on your shoulders or upper chest as the crossed arms settle into place.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your own body while the arms stay folded.
Soften your shoulders and relax your expression, as if settling in for a quiet pause.
tip: “Rests” is signed with the base REST sign.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, keeping the fingers loosely spread and natural.
Lift both arms and cross them over your chest, the right hand coming to rest near the left shoulder.
Land both open hands gently on your shoulders or upper chest as the crossed arms settle into place.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your own body while the arms stay folded.
Soften your shoulders and relax your expression, as if settling in for a quiet pause.
tip: “Resting” is signed with the base REST sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, keeping the fingers loosely spread and natural.
Lift both arms and cross them over your chest, the right hand coming to rest near the left shoulder.
Land both open hands gently on your shoulders or upper chest as the crossed arms settle into place.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your own body while the arms stay folded.
Soften your shoulders and relax your expression, as if settling in for a quiet pause.
tip: Past form of “Rest” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands at the two smaller knuckles, keeping the hands relaxed and natural.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, palms facing each other a few inches apart.
Bring the hands together twice, letting the fingers meet lightly each time.
Keep your palms facing each other and the movement even and unhurried.
Use a warm, neutral expression — the joining motion shows two people pairing up.
tip: Plural of “Partner” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Cup your non-dominant hand loosely and hold it in front of your waist as a container.
Hold your dominant hand flat above it, fingers together, as if carrying items to put inside.
Bring your dominant hand down and tuck it into the cupped hand, pressing the items in.
Repeat the pressing-down motion once more to show packing things firmly together.
Keep the hands angled toward each other during the tucking motion.
Keep a neutral face; the sign reads like physically filling a box or bag.
tip: “Packing” is signed with the base PACK sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant forearm horizontally across your body with the palm facing down.
Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers extended and held together.
Place the edge of your dominant hand on the forearm, close to your body.
Sweep your dominant flat hand outward along the top of the forearm.
Keep the palm facing down the whole time so the hand reads as a flat platform.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral throughout the sign.
tip: Plural of “Stage” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing upward.
With your dominant hand, form the letter B and touch it to the open palm.
Change the dominant hand to the letter G and tap it onto the palm.
Keep the two letters close together, spelling B-G in one flowing motion.
Keep the base palm steady and facing the ceiling while you spell.
Use a matter-of-fact expression; the sign means personal history or context.
tip: Plural of “Background” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make both hands into A handshapes, with thumbs resting against the fists.
Hold the fists up near your shoulders, a few inches from your body.
Thrust both fists downward together in a short, firm motion.
Repeat the downward thrust once more to show established ability.
Keep your palms facing downward or inward through the movement.
Hold your head high with a confident expression as you sign it.
tip: Plural of “Ability” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make both hands flat, fingers extended and held together.
Hold the hands out in front of your body, off to your dominant side.
Sweep both hands together toward your non-dominant side, as if carrying a load.
Repeat the carrying sweep to show the ongoing act of moving.
Keep both palms facing downward as the hands travel across.
Look in the direction the hands travel, like watching boxes being carried.
tip: “Movings” is signed with the base MOVING sign.

steps: Form your non-dominant hand into an S and hold it steady in front of you.
Shape your dominant hand into an open five, fingers together, palm down.
Press the dominant hand down onto the S hand, pushing it downward.
Repeat the downward press once more, for a total of two presses.
Keep the base hand fixed in place while the top hand does the pushing.
Show a little tension in your face and shoulders, as if straining.
tip: Plural of “Pressure” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and close the other fingers.
Jab the fingertip down into the upturned palm like pointing at an amount due.
Repeat the jab once more, for a total of two firm downward pokes.
Keep the palm hand steady and flat while the dominant hand does the jabbing.
Hold a serious expression, as if reminding someone of money owed.
tip: Plural of “Debt” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with fingertips together, like the starting position of the PLEASE sign.
Place your right flat hand on your upper chest and your left flat hand on your belly, an inch or two out from your body.
Circle both hands at the same time in opposite directions, with the right hand looping clockwise and the left hand counterclockwise.
Angle your palms inward toward your torso so the fingertips of each hand point toward the other hand.
Wear a warm, content smile while signing, since the sign conveys pleasure and delight.
tip: “Enjoys” is signed with the base ENJOY sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Hover your dominant hand above it in a loose, relaxed open shape with the palm facing down.
Sweep your dominant hand toward your flat palm, close it into a fist as it touches, then pull it away.
Let the dominant hand drop slightly and reopen into a loose open hand, still palm down.
Keep the palm-down orientation through the whole motion — the hand only opens and closes, it never turns over.
tip: “Removes” is signed with the base REMOVE sign.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you in a flat handshape, palm facing up.
Shape your dominant hand into the letter X, hooking your index finger with the palm facing back toward you.
Bring the top of your hooked index finger down onto your flat palm with one firm downward tap.
Keep the striking hand palm-back as it lands on your non-dominant palm.
Use a neutral, businesslike expression, as if naming a price.
tip: Plural of “Fee” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Start READ by extending your dominant index and middle fingers, holding them like two eyes scanning a page.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you to act as the page being read.
Move your two reading fingertips downward once along the flat page hand.
Finish with the AGENT marker: hold both hands flat with palms facing inward toward your torso.
Move both flat hands downward together past your chest to name 'a person who reads'.
Keep a neutral expression while the AGENT suffix does the grammatical work.
tip: Plural of “Reader” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand near the side of your forehead with your fingers extended and relaxed.
Touch or hover at your temple, just beside your forehead.
Wiggle your fingers in one small fluttering movement; a single wiggle is enough.
Prefer this non-initialized version over the T-handshape variant, which some signers still use.
Wear a thoughtful, serious expression, matching the weight of an abstract idea.
tip: Plural of “Theory” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make a fist with your dominant hand, keeping the thumb extended upward like a thumbs-up.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing upward.
Rest the dominant fist on top of the open non-dominant palm, keeping contact between them.
Lift both hands upward together in one smooth motion, as if raising support to someone.
Keep a warm, open expression that matches the idea of offering assistance.
tip: “Aiding” is signed with the base AID sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Make a fist with your dominant hand, keeping the thumb extended upward like a thumbs-up.

steps: Hook your dominant index finger over your thumb to form an X handshape, folding the remaining fingers down.
Place the hooked X hand just under your chin, close to the front of your throat.
Flick the X hand forward about three inches with a quick motion of the wrist.
Repeat the forward flick one more time, for a total of two quick flicks.
Keep your palm angled slightly downward as the hand flicks away from your throat.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply names the material.
tip: Plural of “Steel” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat with the fingers together, except for the middle and index fingers.
Position your dominant hand so its index finger points at the base of the other hand's middle and index fingers.
Touch the tip of the dominant index finger to the spot where those two fingers meet.
Twist the dominant hand with a small turning motion, as if turning a key.
Keep the twisting finger's palm facing sideways and your expression alert and ready.
tip: Plural of “Beginning” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form an "R" handshape with your dominant hand by crossing your middle finger over your index finger.
Place the R hand at your forehead with the fingertips near your temple, like saluting an idea.
Move your hand forward and slightly outward away from your forehead in one smooth, deliberate motion.
Keep your palm facing sideways toward your other side as the hand travels forward through the air.
Pair the movement with a sincere, dignified expression when honoring someone's worth or status.
tip: “Respects” is signed with the base RESPECT sign.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand into a relaxed curved shape, keeping your thumb extended.
Hold the curved hand at chest height in the signing space in front of your torso.
Sweep the hand in one big arching movement, pushing forward and over toward your non-dominant side.
Keep your palm angled downward through the whole arc, like skimming over a hilltop.
Watch along the path of the movement, as if following your own journey.
tip: Plural of “Trip” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands into loose hooks, like two clasps ready to link.
Bring both hooked hands together at mid-chest, interlocking the fingers of one hand with the other.
Slide the linked hands back and forth against each other in a short cooperative sawing motion.
Keep your palms facing each other while the hooked fingers stay interlocked.
Hold a warm, engaged expression — the sign also means COOPERATION, so show the teamwork.
tip: Plural of “Relationship” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand with your thumb sticking out to the side.
Touch your thumb to one side of your chin, letting your fingers spread across your jaw.
Wipe the thumb across your chin to the other side in one smooth motion, like wiping away sweat.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your body through the whole wipe.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — this is a plain noun, not an insult.
tip: Plural of “Farm” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Interlace the fingers of both hands together, clasping them into one settled bundle.
Hold the clasped hands at mid-chest, a few inches out from your body.
Keep the hands still and quiet — there is no travel; the stillness is the meaning.
Let your palms face each other while the fingers stay interlaced.
Soften your face into a calm, serene expression with relaxed shoulders.
tip: Plural of “Peace” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with the fingers together and extended.
Hold your non-dominant flat hand steady at chest height in front of you.
Rest your dominant flat hand just above it, then sweep it in a small arc over the top, as if smoothing the school grounds.
Keep both of your palms facing downward through the whole sweeping arc.
Use a calm, neutral expression, like a guide describing the school grounds.
tip: Plural of “Campus” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve the fingers of your dominant hand into a C shape, thumb opposite your fingertips.
Hold the C hand at chest height in front of your torso.
Close the C down into a fist in one smooth motion, letting the fingers curl shut.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your body as the hand closes.
Keep your face neutral and descriptive, as if naming a place on a map.
tip: Plural of “Coast” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both index fingers into hooked "X" handshapes, like loose fists with only the index fingers bent.
Hold the hooked hands near your chest with your palms facing upward toward the recipient.
Move both hands forward and slightly downward in one smooth arc, as if bestowing something on another person.
Keep your palms angled upward through the movement, ending with both hands extended forward.
Wear a serious, formal facial expression that matches the official tone of granting an award.
tip: “Grants” is signed with the base GRANT sign.

steps: Curl both index fingers into hooked "X" handshapes, like loose fists with only the index fingers bent.

steps: Touch your dominant index finger to your temple with your palm facing inward, like the sign for thinking.
Hook both index fingers and bring your dominant hand down to meet your non-dominant hand.
Let the two hooked fingers touch and interlock briefly in front of your chest.
Nod your head once as the hands meet, confirming 'yes, we are in agreement.'
Keep both palms angled toward each other and hold a positive, confirming facial expression.
tip: “Agrees” is signed with the base AGREE sign.

steps: Point your dominant index finger toward your face, holding it a few inches from your nose.
Sweep the index finger sideways past your nose in one smooth motion without ever touching it.
Keep your palm facing sideways and your finger held rigid as it crosses in front of your face.
Drive the movement from your wrist or elbow in a single confident pass across the midline.
Pair the sign with a neutral face, and add the INVENT sign for 'invented story' when you need extra clarity.
tip: Plural of “Fiction” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend your dominant index finger into a slight hook, like a small tapping finger.
Tap the side of your ear twice with the tip of your hooked index finger.
Keep your palm facing outward and your elbow relaxed at your side while you tap.
Use a light, quick double-tap right at the ear opening for a clean production.
Keep your face neutral and your eyes on your conversation partner.
tip: “Hears” is signed with the base HEAR sign.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a loose fist, as if gripping a short pencil.
Touch the fist to your mouth, like wetting a pencil tip before taking notes.
Bring the fist down onto the flat, upturned palm of your non-dominant hand.
Mime quick writing strokes across that open palm, as if writing on paper.
Keep the non-dominant palm level and facing up while the fist writes on it.
Hold a calm, attentive expression, like someone taking dictation from a boss.
tip: Plural of “Secretary” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into loose fists, resting your thumbs across the top.
Hold the fists at chest height, about a shoulder-width apart in neutral space.
Turn both palms to face each other so the fists mirror one another.
Push both fists straight forward together in one smooth, level motion.
Freeze the fist shapes as they travel, like paving a stretch of road.
Keep your face neutral — this one sign covers street, way, path, and road.
tip: Plural of “Path” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat, spreading only the index and middle fingers.
Place your dominant index finger at the base of those two spread fingers.
Twist the dominant index finger once, as if turning a small key.
Let the twisting finger's palm face sideways during the turning motion.
Wear an alert, ready expression that matches a fresh beginning.
tip: “Begins” is signed with the base BEGIN sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an open hand with the thumb extended outward.
Touch your thumb firmly against the side of your forehead near the temple.
Sweep your hand straight down until the thumb lands flat on your chest.
Keep your palm angled toward your opposite side while the hand travels downward.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, since the sign needs no special facial grammar.
tip: Plural of “Guy” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into loose open-F handshapes, each thumb tip resting against its index fingertip.
Hold your hands apart in the signing space in front of your chest.
Bring both hands toward each other and hook the fingers together into interlocking F shapes.
Angle your palms toward each other so the hooked fingers cross like two chain links.
End with a brief firm hold, adding a small nod when used as a statement.
tip: “Connects” is signed with the base CONNECT sign.
